q: בת 84 מגיעה למרפאה לאחר שנפלה בביתה מספר פעמים. בהערכה עולה כי היא סובלת מאינסומניה מזה כעשר שנים, מאז מות בעלה. מאז מטופלת ב- BROTIZOLAM (BONDORMIN). היא העלתה את המינון על דעת עצמה עד ל- 2 כדורים ללילה. היא מדווחת על מצב רוח שמור ובסקר GDS צברה ניקוד של 3/15. מה הצעד הבא להמשך הטיפול?
o: הפסקה מידית של BROTIZOLAM בעקבות הנפילות, גם במחיר של הפרעה בשינה
החלפה של הטיפול מ- BROTIZOLAM ל- TRAZODIL
הפחתה הדרגתית של הטיפול ב BROTIZOLAM ובמקביל הפניה לטיפול קוגניטיבי התנהגותי להפרעות שינה
הערכה במעבדת שינה לקביעת דפוס השינה והתאמת טיפול תרופתי
explanation:
Brotizolam is a benzodiazepine hypnotic. Ten years of use, dose escalation and recurrent falls favor **a supervised gradual taper paired with cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I)**.

**A. Abrupt discontinuation** Long-term exposure can produce physical dependence. Stopping suddenly risks withdrawal and rebound insomnia.
**B. Switch to trazodone** Sedation and orthostatic hypotension could compound her fall risk, and changing sedatives leaves the chronic insomnia untreated.
**C. Taper and start CBT-I** Reduce the drug gradually while addressing the thoughts, routines and bed–wake associations that perpetuate insomnia.
**D. Perform a sleep study** Typical chronic insomnia is assessed clinically. The immediate problems are the escalating hypnotic and the falls.

q: A clinically stable woman has undergone surgical repair of a hip fracture. What approach to postoperative mobility does Hazzard recommend?
o: Begin mobilization by the first postoperative day.
Wait for radiographic union of the fracture.
Begin mobilization after completion of inpatient rehabilitation.
Maintain bed rest until pain has resolved.
explanation:
Early movement after a stable hip repair helps limit deconditioning, pneumonia, pressure injury and venous thrombosis. **Mobilize on the day of surgery if possible and by the first postoperative day.**

**A. Begin mobilization by the first postoperative day** — Assist the patient with transfers and walking as tolerated under the surgical weight-bearing plan.
**B. Wait for radiographic union of the fracture** — Union takes far longer than the safe interval for initial mobilization after a stable repair.
**C. Begin mobilization after completion of inpatient rehabilitation** — Movement is part of acute postoperative care and continues throughout rehabilitation.
**D. Maintain bed rest until pain has resolved** — Treat pain to permit activity. Prolonged bed rest while pain persists increases complications.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 797.

q: An 85-year-old man with heart failure, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease has a PSA of 12 ng/mL and an abnormal digital rectal examination. Biopsy reveals prostate adenocarcinoma with a Gleason score of 7. He has been hospitalized twice this year for heart-failure exacerbations, needs help with activities of daily living, and has an estimated life expectancy of 2–3 years. He has no urinary symptoms. His care plan is to defer cancer treatment until symptomatic disease develops. Which strategy does this describe?
o: Definitive treatment by radical prostatectomy
Definitive treatment by external beam radiation
Watchful waiting with treatment for symptomatic disease
Active surveillance with delayed potentially curative treatment
explanation:
Severe competing illness and a short life expectancy favor a symptom-directed strategy when that matches the patient’s goals. **Deferring treatment until symptomatic disease is watchful waiting**.

**A. Radical prostatectomy.** Surgery would begin curative-intent local treatment immediately.
**B. External-beam radiation.** Definitive irradiation treats the localized cancer before symptoms emerge.
**C. Watchful waiting.** Treatment is reserved for symptoms that affect comfort or function.
**D. Active surveillance.** More intensive monitoring aims to detect progression early enough for delayed cure.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1414.

. External-beam radiation.** Definitive irradiation treats the localized cancer before symptoms emerge.
. Watchful waiting.** Treatment is reserved for symptoms that affect comfort or function.

q: A 78-year-old woman living alone has unintentionally lost 8 lb over six months. Her appetite has declined and food no longer tastes the same. She takes lisinopril, metformin, sertraline, and omeprazole; BMI is 20 kg/m2. Which approach incorporates the nutritional screening and medication review described in Hazzard?
o: Obtain metabolic and thyroid tests in place of assessing weight change and food intake
Perform MNA and review medications affecting taste or appetite
Arrange endoscopy in place of assessing nutritional status and medication effects
Prescribe calorie supplements and postpone nutritional assessment for three months
explanation:
Unintentional weight loss can reveal inadequate intake before an older adult looks malnourished. Changes in appetite and taste make a medication history part of the assessment.
**Use the Mini Nutritional Assessment and review medicines that may impair taste or appetite.**

**A. Laboratory tests alone.** Metabolic and thyroid tests may help identify an illness but leave actual intake and weight trajectory unmeasured.
**B. Nutritional screen and medication review.** This documents nutritional risk while addressing a potentially reversible contributor.
**C. Proceed directly to endoscopy.** Endoscopy may follow specific clinical findings. It does not assess nutritional risk or medication effects.
**D. Supplements and delayed assessment.** Delaying evaluation overlooks continued weight loss and treatable causes of poor intake.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 166, Nutrition and Table 11-3.

q: A 75-year-old woman taking sertraline, an SSRI, is prescribed tramadol after a fracture. Which drug-related syndrome does Hazzard identify as a risk of combining tramadol with this antidepressant class?
o: Risk of neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Risk of drug-induced serotonin syndrome
Risk of opioid withdrawal syndrome
Risk of acute anticholinergic syndrome
explanation:
Tramadol relieves pain through opioid activity and also inhibits serotonin reuptake. Adding it to sertraline increases serotonergic activity and puts this woman at risk for **serotonin syndrome**.

**A. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome.** Marked rigidity after dopamine blockade or abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic therapy points to this syndrome.
**B. Serotonin syndrome.** New clonus and brisk reflexes, often with agitation or sweating, would point to serotonin toxicity after tramadol is added.
**C. Opioid withdrawal.** Withdrawal follows a reduction or interruption of opioid exposure in a dependent patient. Here an opioid is being added.
**D. Anticholinergic toxicity.** Dry skin and urinary retention are characteristic of muscarinic blockade. The interaction between these drugs involves serotonergic signaling.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1653.
ref: Hazzard Ch 103 — FIBROMYALGIA AND MYOFASCIAL PAIN SYNDROMES

. Opioid withdrawal.** Withdrawal follows a reduction or interruption of opioid exposure in a dependent patient. Here an opioid is being added.
. Anticholinergic toxicity.** Dry skin and urinary retention are characteristic of muscarinic blockade. The interaction between these drugs involves serotonergic signaling.

q: A nursing-home resident continues to fall despite physiotherapy. She uses a walker and has cognitive impairment. Which approach is appropriate for further assessment of her falls risk?
o: Repeat cognitive testing and adapt supervision
Assess the range of modifiable fall risks
Measure bone density and address fracture risk
Evaluate walker fit and transfer technique
explanation:
Continued falls despite physiotherapy suggest other important contributors may remain. **Perform a multifactorial assessment and use it to individualize the prevention plan.**

**A. Base the plan on cognition** — Cognitive impairment matters, particularly with impulsive transfers, but medication effects and standing balance also merit assessment.
**B. Assess several domains** — Observe how she stands, transfers and uses the walker. Review her falls, drugs, behaviors and environment with staff.
**C. Base it on bone density** — Bone density helps assess fracture risk if she falls. It does not explain repeated loss of balance.
**D. Base it on walker use** — The walker provides one clue to mobility limitations. It cannot quantify all contributing deficits or distinguish their causes.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 637–638 and 641.

q: An 83-year-old woman in rehabilitation after a hip fracture cries, eats little, and says she wants to die. Her evaluation is not yet complete. What should be included immediately in suicide-risk assessment?
o: Suicidal thoughts, intent, plans, and access to means
Appetite, weight, sleep habits, and daily protein intake
Pain, range of motion, strength, and rehabilitation participation
Memory, orientation, daily function, and family dependence
explanation:
A wish to die after hip fracture may reflect pain, grief, depression or active suicidal intent. Safety assessment belongs in the first conversation while medical and psychiatric evaluation proceeds.
**Ask about current thoughts, intent, plans and access to means, and establish whether she can remain safe.**

**A. Direct suicide assessment.** Clarify the meaning and immediacy of the statement. Prior behavior, protective supports and direct observation also guide disposition.
**B. Nutritional assessment.** Poor appetite and weight loss deserve evaluation. They cannot identify whether she intends to act.
**C. Pain and rehabilitation assessment.** Treat pain and address loss of independence alongside the immediate safety assessment.
**D. Cognitive and family assessment.** Cognition and support influence the plan. Neither substitutes for asking directly about suicidal thoughts and access.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1013, 1017–1018, Figure 65-3

q: A 76-year-old woman with COPD has an FEV1 of 45% predicted, sarcopenia with a grip strength of 14 kg, and increasing difficulty bathing independently despite optimized bronchodilator therapy. She has lost 8 lb over 6 months; BMI is 19.2 and albumin is 3.1 g/dL. She asks about prognosis and hospice. Which assessment combines nutritional status, airflow obstruction, dyspnea, and exercise capacity to inform the prognosis discussion?
o: Calculate the multidimensional BODE index
Measure her six-minute walking distance
Repeat spirometry to reassess airflow limitation
Perform a standardized depression screening assessment
explanation:
Airflow obstruction alone gives an incomplete prognosis. Walking ability, nutritional reserve and the patient's experience of dyspnea contribute independent information.
**Calculate the BODE index using body mass index, airflow obstruction, dyspnea and exercise capacity.**

**A. BODE index.** Combine BMI, FEV₁, a dyspnea scale and six-minute walking distance. Use the result alongside her functional losses and goals.
**B. Six-minute walking distance.** This measures exercise capacity, one of the four components.
**C. Repeat spirometry.** FEV₁ measures airflow obstruction but misses exercise tolerance, nutritional status and perceived breathlessness.
**D. Depression screening.** Mood deserves assessment but a depression scale does not measure the four requested domains.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1245–1246.

q: איזה אביזר עזר מומלץ למטופל קטוע רגל לפני התאמת פרוטזה?
o: רולטור (ROLLATOR)
הליכון עם 4 גלגלים (4 – WHEELED ROLLING WALKER)
הליכון עם 2 גלגלים (2 – WHEELED ROLLING WALKER)
הליכון סטנדרטי ללא גלגלים (STANDART "PICK-UP" WALKER)
explanation:
Before prosthetic fitting, a unilateral leg amputee may need to support substantial body weight through the arms while advancing on the intact limb. A stable frame allows this transfer of load without rolling forward.

**A standard pick-up walker without wheels is the best choice among these devices. Its four stationary feet provide the most stable support while the residual limb is unloaded.**

**A. Rollator.** A rollator is a four-wheeled walker. It is useful for outdoor mobility or seated rest but can roll under heavy loading.
**B. Four-wheeled walker.** This describes the same device as a rollator. Free movement of the wheels makes it a poor choice for lifting and supporting body weight through the frame.
**C. Two-wheeled walker.** The rear contact points improve stability compared with four wheels, but the front wheels still move. A stationary frame better suits complete limb unloading.
**D. Standard pick-up walker.** Once all four feet are planted, the frame remains still as the patient supports weight through the arms and advances the intact leg.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 827–828, Table 55-5.

q: Before using the rheumatoid-arthritis classification score in Hazzard Table 101-1, which clinical entry conditions must be met?
o: Joint pain may replace clinical synovitis when rheumatoid factor is positive
Clinical synovitis qualifies even when another disease explains it better
Positive anti-CCP antibodies qualify even without any clinical joint synovitis
Definite clinical synovitis must be present without a better alternative explanation
explanation:
The RA classification score estimates the likelihood of rheumatoid arthritis in a patient with **clinical synovitis in at least one joint that another diagnosis does not explain better**.

**A. Joint pain may replace clinical synovitis when rheumatoid factor is positive.** Pain alone can occur without synovial inflammation. Positive rheumatoid factor cannot replace a swollen joint.
**B. Clinical synovitis qualifies even when another disease explains it better.** A more convincing diagnosis, such as crystal arthritis, must be considered before applying the score.
**C. Positive anti-CCP antibodies qualify even without any clinical joint synovitis.** Anti-CCP contributes points after the patient meets the clinical entry conditions.
**D. Definite clinical synovitis must be present without a better alternative explanation.** Definite synovitis and the absence of a better explanation are both required before counting joints or scoring serology.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1608.

q: In the small anti-CCP study cited by Hazzard, which pattern distinguished late-onset rheumatoid arthritis (LORA) from polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR)?
o: Similar positivity in LORA, PMR and healthy controls.
65% positivity in PMR and none in LORA or controls.
Positivity in every LORA patient and none with PMR.
65% positivity in LORA and none in PMR or controls.
explanation:
Late-onset rheumatoid arthritis can resemble polymyalgia rheumatica through shoulder pain and stiffness. **Anti-CCP positivity favored RA** in this small comparison.

**A. Similar positivity in LORA, PMR and healthy controls** — Identical positivity would not distinguish the groups. Antibodies were detected only in the RA group.
**B. 65% positivity in PMR and none in LORA or controls** — The 65% figure belongs to late-onset RA. The PMR group had no positive results.
**C. Positivity in every LORA patient and none with PMR** — Sensitivity was incomplete. About one-third of the patients with RA tested negative.
**D. 65% positivity in LORA and none in PMR or controls** — Positivity in 65% of the RA group and none of the PMR or control groups makes a positive result informative. A negative result cannot exclude RA.

Reference · Hazzard 8e Ch 101 - p1611

q: How do you distinguish neurogenic claudication from vascular claudication on exercise testing?
o: Both conditions resolve on the treadmill because spinal extension increases canal diameter
Both conditions improve on the bicycle because spinal flexion reduces vascular symptoms
Neurogenic symptoms improve on the bicycle; vascular symptoms persist on both tests
Neurogenic symptoms persist on both tests; vascular symptoms improve on the bicycle
explanation:
Neurogenic claudication is exertional leg discomfort from lumbar spinal stenosis that varies with spinal posture. **Cycling in a flexed position often relieves neurogenic symptoms. Vascular claudication can occur on both tests** when the leg workload is sufficient.

**A. Both improve on the treadmill.** Lumbar extension narrows the canal, so upright walking can provoke neurogenic leg symptoms.
**B. Both improve on the bicycle.** Leaning forward widens the spinal canal but cannot correct limited arterial blood flow to exercising muscles.
**C. Bicycle relief favors neurogenic pain.** Improvement when the patient bends forward while continuing to pedal points to posture-dependent neural compression.
**D. Bicycle relief favors vascular pain.** Vascular symptoms improve when muscular demand falls with rest. Changing spinal posture alone offers little relief.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1636.

q:
בן 71, ברקע Cardiac Cirrhosis, אי ספיקת כליות עם קריאטנין בסיס סביב 2 mg/dL. מתאשפז בשל דה-קומפנסציה כבדית ומיימת קשה.

מהי הפרעת החומצה בסיס ממנה סובל המטופל?
o: Normal Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis משולב עם Respiratory Alkalosis
Normal Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis
High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis
High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis משולב עם Metabolic Alkalosis
keySource: IMA 2024-Sep Basic official answer key after appeals, Q139
explanation:
Albumin is a major unmeasured anion. A very low albumin can hide an increased anion gap. **High-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation** fits these values after correcting for albumin.

**A. Normal-gap acidosis plus respiratory alkalosis.** PCO₂ of 37 is in the expected compensatory range of about 36 to 40 for bicarbonate 20. There is no separate respiratory alkalosis shown.
**B. Normal-gap acidosis alone.** The uncorrected gap is 10, but albumin is only 2.1. Treating this as an uncorrected normal gap misses retained unmeasured acids.
**C. High-gap metabolic acidosis.** Using albumin 4.5 as the reference, the correction adds about 6 to the measured gap, yielding approximately 16.
**D. High-gap acidosis plus metabolic alkalosis.** A separate metabolic alkalosis is not required to explain the bicarbonate and compensated PCO₂ in this vignette.

Reference · Harrison 22e, pp. 367–368.

q: במטופל עם חשד לאנצפליטיס על רקע HERPES SIMPLEX VIRUS (HSV) איזה מהמשפטים הבאים נכון בנוגע לבדיקות לצורך האבחנה?
o: ב- MRI נראה שינויים דיפוזיים בחומר הלבן
PCR עשוי להיות שלילי ב- 72 השעות הראשונות
סרולוגיה חיובית בדם מסייעת באבחון זיהום זה
תרבית CSF שלילית ל- HSV שוללת זיהום זה
keySource: IMA 2024-May Basic official answer key after appeals, Q140
explanation:
When HSV encephalitis is suspected, CSF HSV PCR is the preferred diagnostic test. **An early negative PCR during the first 72 hours can be misleading**, so persistent clinical concern warrants repeat testing and continued empiric acyclovir.

**A. Diffuse white-matter disease.** HSV more often produces asymmetric temporal, insular or adjacent cortical abnormalities.
**B. Early false-negative PCR.** Viral DNA may become detectable on a later CSF sample.
**C. Positive serum serology.** Common background HSV exposure limits the specificity of serum antibodies for current encephalitis.
**D. Negative CSF culture.** Culture is insensitive in HSV encephalitis and a negative result cannot rule it out.

Reference · Harrison 22e, pp. 1112–1113.

. Early false-negative PCR.** Viral DNA may become detectable on a later CSF sample.
. Positive serum serology.** Common background HSV exposure limits the specificity of serum antibodies for current encephalitis.
. Negative CSF culture.** Culture is insensitive in HSV encephalitis and a negative result cannot rule it out.

explanationParts.text: When HSV encephalitis is suspected, CSF HSV PCR is the preferred diagnostic test. **An early negative PCR during the first 72 hours can be misleading**, so persistent clinical concern warrants repeat testing and continued empiric acyclovir.
Reference · Harrison 22e, pp. 1112–1113.
